summary:
Crater Expectations is a game about choosing where to land at the Moon's south pole, made for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. The ground is built from NASA LRO laser altimetry (LOLA), lightly smoothed so it can be played, covering the ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache craters, an Artemis III candidate region. The Sun and Earth follow their real 2027 paths from NASA JPL Horizons.

At the pole the Sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon, so a ridge 40 km away can block it. Players scout from orbit, read a 360° skyline, compare sites by sunlight, Earth contact and slope, and pick a landing hour. Then they fly the landing and drive a rover on missions that make those trade-offs real: work in sunlight, send data while Earth is in view, and risk dark craters for ice while solar storms threaten. A Planner Mode shows a best-sites heat map and tests what happens if the launch slips. A validation screen checks the game's numbers against published studies and Horizons data.

It matters because it turns the hard, invisible reasons a landing site is chosen into something anyone can see
details:
Crater Expectations

Team: Outrstelr: Mahmoud Balash · Ayman Negm · Anas Abdullah · Mohamed Badawi · Abdulrahman Salem

Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Event: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Cairo

Play it (free, in the browser, no install): https://mvvhmxd.github.io/nasaspaceapps2026/

Demo video (30 s): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Wprdl6JC1BM00_pUoPE-iEbZO0ZB9qTV/view?usp=sharing

Source code: https://github.com/mvvhmxd/nasaspaceapps2026

High-Level Summary

Crater Expectations is a browser game about choosing where to land at the Moon's south pole. There the Sun never rises high: it circles just above the horizon, and the Earth wobbles low in the sky. So a ridge a few kilometres away can decide whether a lander gets power and whether it can talk to Earth.

You scout real terrain from orbit. A live 360° skyline shows where the Sun and Earth really are, and where the ridges hide them. You pick a landing site and hour, fly the landing yourself, and drive a rover to do science before sunset and Earthset. The terrain comes from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter laser altimeter (LOLA). The Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons for real dates in 2027. A Planner Mode lets anyone compare sites and dates directly, and a Validation screen checks the game's numbers against published research.

The goal is to make the trade-offs that mission planners face (sunlight, Earth contact, slope) something anyone can feel and understand in a few minutes.

The Problem

NASA's Artemis program plans to land crews near the lunar south pole. Picking a site there is hard:

- Sunlight is rare and fragile. The Sun sits within a degree or two of the horizon. Solar power depends on whether the local skyline lets the Sun through, hour by hour.

- Earth contact comes and goes. Talking to Earth directly needs the Earth above the local ridges. A site with great sunlight may lose Earth for days.

- Slope and shadow matter. A lander needs gentle ground. Permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice, but they are cold and dark.

- Schedules slip. A launch that slips a day can turn a good site into a bad one.

Planning tools for this exist, but they are made for experts. Students, educators and the public rarely get to see why one site beats another.

Our Solution

Crater Expectations turns the site-selection problem into a short, playable mission. Instead of reading a table, you watch the Sun drop behind a ridge and feel the clock running.

1. Scout from orbit

You fly a scout over a top-down map of the real terrain around Connecting Ridge, an Artemis III candidate region. A 360° skyline strip updates from wherever you hover, showing the true Sun and Earth and the ridges that block them. You can plant up to 3 flags and compare each site's sunlit share and Earth visibility. You can also scrub time to preview how the sky moves, then choose your landing spot and hour.

2. Fly the landing

You fly the last 260 m of the descent yourself, in a 3D chase view over the real LOLA terrain under the real Sun angle. You manage throttle, tilt and fuel. The touchdown limits are under 2 m/s down, 1.5 m/s sideways, 8° of tilt and a slope under 15°. An optional autopilot costs points, and a free landing assist keeps new players from crashing.

3. Drive the rover and race the horizon

On the surface you drive a rover in a first-person view. The view is ray-marched from the height map, with real cast shadows. You work stations under the sky you chose:

- Survey: needs sunlight.

- Dish: needs the Earth above the ridge to send your science home.

- Drill: pays more in shadow but drains the battery.

Time to sunset and to Earthset hangs in the sky above the horizon. The battery drains in the dark and cold. You must be back at the lander for the ascent window, or the crew is left behind.

4. Three missions, each harder than the last

Mission 1, Learn the Horizon, asks you to work where the Sun reaches. It teaches that sunlight depends on the local skyline, not just the time of day.

Mission 2, Get It Home, asks you to send your data while the Earth is still up. Science only counts once it is transmitted, so you race Earthset.

Mission 3, The Trade-Off, sends you after ice in the dark. Permanently shadowed ground holds ice but drains power. A 12-hour launch slip moves the whole sky, and solar storms force you to shelter.

Each mission starts you somewhere imperfect on purpose (half-lit, losing Earth, a dark hollow), with less battery and a higher science target.

5. Debrief: your site vs the planner's pick

After each mission, six KPIs are graded A to F against targets:

- science sent home

- crew home

- lander sunlit %

- dish Earth %

- lowest battery

- science left unsent

The debrief then compares your landing site's Sun and Earth timeline with the best of all the landable sites on the map, and explains why one is better. This is how a real site planner thinks.

6. Planner Mode (press P on the title screen)

A direct navigator for planners, teachers and the curious:

- Pick any hour of 2027, with hour, day and week steps and a time-lapse.

- Choose from named published sites or type a latitude/longitude.

- Compare up to 3 sites by Sun %, Earth %, Sun clearance and next sunset/Earthset.

- Run a schedule-slip test (+1 day, +3 days, +7 days).

- See a "best sites" heat map.

A short walkthrough opens the first time.

7. Validation screen (press V on the title screen)

We show our work. The game recomputes its numbers and puts them next to published and independent values:

- Sunlight at 4 published sites (Connecting Ridge and Shackleton rim, from Gläser et al. 2017) vs the game's computed sunlight. Mean difference: 4.3 percentage points with raw LOLA and 2.9 points as played.

- Sun and Earth elevation vs independent JPL Horizons topocentric queries at 8 dates in 2027. Largest difference: 0.005°, for comparison the Sun's disc is 0.53° wide.

- Permanent shadow check: the floor of Shackleton crater stays shadowed all year in the game, matching published work (Zuber et al. 2012).

8. Made for first-timers

- A numbered walkthrough explains the controls, the live numbers and what makes a good landing site. Press H to replay it.

- Radio calls from CAPCOM, the Commander and the Lunar Module Pilot are voiced over walkie-talkie static.

- Generative music follows the sky: warm in sunlight, cold in shadow, a "home" melody while Earth is visible, and tension near sunset, Earthset or low battery.

How We Used NASA Data

LOLA polar elevation maps. We use LDEM_85S_40M (40 m per pixel) and LDEM_75S_240M (240 m per pixel) from the NASA LRO LOLA team, through the PDS Geosciences Node. They give the terrain you fly over and drive on, the skyline that blocks the Sun and Earth, cast shadows, slope and permanently shadowed ground. Lunar curvature is included.

JPL Horizons ephemeris. From NASA JPL Solar System Dynamics we use the Moon's sub-solar and sub-Earth points, hourly for 2027 (DE441). They place the Sun and Earth in the sky for each mission's real 2027 date and for every hour in Planner Mode. A full year of Sun positions marks which ground never sees the Sun.

JPL Horizons topocentric queries. Independent Sun and Earth positions at 8 dates in 2027, also from NASA JPL Solar System Dynamics, provide the check values on the Validation screen.

Gläser et al. 2017, "Illumination conditions at the lunar poles" (NASA Technical Reports Server, NTRS 20170007365). Its published sunlight percentages are used for validation.

Zuber et al. 2012 (Shackleton crater). This published research is used for the permanent-shadow check.

Other data: Natural Earth 1:110m land outlines (public domain), used to draw the continents on the Earth disc.

Honesty about the data

We say each of these on screen:

- Smoothed for play. The LOLA heights are blended halfway toward a smoothed copy so the rover can drive the terrain. Every credit line says "smoothed for play", and the Validation screen shows results for both the raw and the as-played terrain.

- Exaggerated views. The first-person views stretch heights ×3 vertically so ridges read clearly, and this is marked on screen. The Earth is drawn larger than real, and its night side is brightened so you can still see it. Both are labelled.

- Game physics. Rover, battery, lander, cargo and solar-storm behaviour are a simplified game model, not engineering simulations.

Benefits and Impact

- For the public and students: a 5-minute, hands-on way to understand why Artemis landing sites are chosen where they are. No install, it works in any browser and runs offline once loaded.

- For educators: Planner Mode and the Validation screen turn the game into a lesson about light, shadow, orbits and data checking, with real NASA data and visible sources.

- For planners: a fast, intuitive way to compare sites and dates and test schedule slips, directly addressing the challenge's goals.

- Data literacy: it shows how public NASA data can be used, checked and honestly adapted, including where a game simplifies.

How We Built It

- Game: a single offline web page in plain JavaScript with no game engine. The graphics are drawn on an HTML canvas in a high-detail ASCII / dot-matrix style: every image, including the logo, terrain, Sun, Earth, lander, rover and HUD, is generated by code from the data. There are no image files.

- 3D views: a ray-marched height map with real sun-angle shading and cast shadows.

- Sound: music and effects synthesized live with the Web Audio API. The radio voices are pre-recorded synthetic speech run through a walkie-talkie filter (ffmpeg).

- Data pipeline: Node.js scripts download the LOLA maps and JPL Horizons tables and bake them into one compact file the game loads offline.

- Hosting: GitHub Pages, deployed automatically by GitHub Actions.

- Demo video: HyperFrames (an HTML-to-video tool), using real gameplay recorded frame by frame from the game.

Limitations and Next Steps

Limitations:

- One terrain region (Connecting Ridge and the surrounding area).

- Planner Mode coordinates are limited to that map.

- The physics is a game model.

- The radio voices are synthetic.

Next steps:

- More south-pole regions, such as other Artemis III candidates.

- Slope and hazard maps from LOLA in Planner Mode.

- Teammates recording the radio lines.

- A classroom worksheet built around Planner Mode.

Declaration of AI Usage

In line with the NASA Space Apps Challenge guidance on AI, we declare the following.

AI tools used

1. an AI coding assistant. Under our team's direction it was used to:

- write some of the game's source code (rendering, 3D views, rover and landing physics, missions, Planner Mode, Validation screen, sound synthesis);

2. Kokoro text-to-speech (an open AI voice model, run locally) generated the narration voice in the demo video.

3. Microsoft Windows built-in speech voices (offline, synthetic) generated the in-game radio voices (CAPCOM, Commander, Lunar Module Pilot). The voices are synthetic, not real people.

Sound is AI-generated

None of the sound was recorded from real people or real instruments.

- The in-game music and sound effects are generated live in the browser by synthesis code written with AI. There are no recorded music files.

- The in-game radio voices are synthetic text-to-speech reading lines written with AI. An AI-written script processes them to sound like a radio.

- The demo video's narration is AI text-to-speech (Kokoro). Its background music and sound effects come from HeyGen's free stock catalog.

- All scientific data comes from NASA and published sources (LOLA, JPL Horizons, Gläser et al. 2017, Zuber et al. 2012). AI did not create, invent or change any data values. The terrain smoothing is a fixed, documented calculation that we disclose on screen, and the Validation screen shows raw and smoothed results side by side.

- No AI-generated images. Every visual is drawn live by the game's code from the data.

- All footage in the demo video is real gameplay.

Verification: we checked the AI-written code by playing the game. We checked the science against independent sources, as shown on the in-game Validation screen. No NASA logos or branding are used.
